title: Distinct Prime Factors of Product of Array
statement:
Multiply together all the values in the array of positive integers `nums`. Return how many different prime numbers divide that product.

A prime is an integer greater than `1` whose only positive divisors are `1` and itself, and a number `d` divides `x` when `x / d` is a whole number.
notes:
## Intuition

The product of up to 10^4 numbers is astronomically large, so never build it. A prime divides a product exactly when it divides at least one of the factors, so the primes of the product are just the union of the primes of each element. Factor every number on its own and collect the primes in a set; the set's size is the answer. (A brute force could try every prime up to 1000 and check whether any element is a multiple of it.)

## Approach

1. Keep a set `primes` of the prime factors seen so far.
2. For each `num`, copy it into `value` and try divisors `factor = 2, 3, ...` while `factor * factor <= value`.
3. While `factor` divides `value`, record it and divide it out. Because smaller factors are removed first, every `factor` that divides here is prime.
4. Whatever is left above `1` has no divisor up to its square root, so it is a prime itself; add it.
5. Return `primes.size`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2,4,3,7,10,6]`. For `2`, the loop never runs (`2 * 2 > 2`) and `value = 2` is added. For `4`, `factor = 2` divides twice, leaving `1`; `2` is already in the set. `3` and `7` are added as leftovers. For `10`, `2` divides once, leaving `5`, and the loop stops because `3 * 3 > 5`, so `5` is added. `6` gives `2` and then the leftover `3`. The set is `{2, 3, 7, 5}`, so the answer is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · √M) with M = 1000: each number is trial-divided up to its square root.
- Space: O(P), where P ≤ 168 is the number of primes up to 1000.

## Pitfalls

- Multiplying the numbers first overflows almost immediately.
- Forgetting the leftover prime after the loop misses factors such as `5` in `10` or `997` itself.
- Count each prime once: in Example 2 the product is `2^10`, which has one distinct prime, not ten. The set takes care of repeats within and across elements.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `primes` | set of distinct primes found in any element |
| `num` | the current element |
| `value` | what remains of `num` after dividing out found factors |
| `factor` | the trial divisor |

narration.2: Collect each prime once, no matter how many elements contain it.
narration.3: A prime divides the product exactly when it divides some element, so factor each element alone.
narration.4: Work on a copy that will shrink as factors are removed.
narration.5: Trial divisors only need to go up to the square root of what remains.
narration.6: While this factor still divides the value...
narration.7: ...record it as a prime of the product...
narration.8: ...and divide it out so larger factors see only what is left.
narration.11: Anything above 1 left over has no smaller divisor, so it is prime.
narration.15: The number of distinct primes collected is the answer.
